q: A continuous footing that supports an entire heavy structure and reduces settlements on weak soil.
n: A mat (raft) footing is a continuous slab under the whole building. It spreads loads over weak soil and reduces settlement. Source: Das, Principles of Foundation Engineering, Ch. 6 (Mat Foundations).

q: A continuous strip of concrete supporting a continuous wall carrying a uniformly distributed load.
n: A strip footing is a continuous strip of concrete under a wall carrying a uniformly distributed load. Source: Das, Principles of Foundation Engineering, Ch. 3.

q: A three-storey commercial building was constructed on a site where the geotechnical investigation was limited. Several months after occupancy, portions of the structure suddenly experienced excessive settlement. Inspection revealed that the soil beneath the footings had sheared and bulged outward, causing a rapid loss of support. Which structural or geotechnical failure most likely occurred?
o: Punching Shear Failure, because concentrated column loads perforated the footing around the column interface.
Bearing Failure, because the supporting soil was unable to sustain the imposed stresses and failed in shear beneath the foundation.
Differential Settlement, because varying soil compressibility caused different portions of the structure to settle at different rates.
Consolidation Settlement, because long-term compression of saturated soil gradually reduced the elevation of the structure.
n: Soil that shears and bulges outward beneath footings, with a sudden loss of support, is a bearing capacity (shear) failure. Source: Das, Principles of Foundation Engineering, Ch. 3 (Bearing Capacity, general shear failure).

q: A mid-rise commercial building is planned on a site where the soil investigation reveals a deep layer of soft clay with low bearing capacity, highly variable
n: A raft spreads loads over the whole footprint. That lowers bearing pressure and evens out differential settlement on soft, variable clay. Source: Das, Principles of Foundation Engineering, Ch. 6.

q: A mid-rise building to be erected in the University Belt area is planned on a site where the upper soil layers consist of loose fill and soft clay extending several meters deep, making shallow foundations impractical. The project also requires minimal vibration during construction because of adjacent old structures and sensitive facilities. The design team needs a deep foundation system that can penetrate through weak strata, reach competent bearing layers, and be installed with very low noise and disturbance. Which foundation system best fits these conditions?
n: Bored (cast-in-place) piles pass through soft strata to competent layers with little noise and vibration, which protects nearby old structures. Source: Das, Principles of Foundation Engineering, Ch. 9 and 11 (Drilled Shafts).

q: A multi-storey hotel is planned on a site underlain by loose alluvial deposits with shallow groundwater. The geotechnical report shows that the upper layers are too weak for shallow foundations and that the structure requires a deep foundation capable of penetrating through variable strata while providing high load capacity and settlement control. The contractor prefers a system that can be installed rapidly and does not rely on soil improvement. Which foundation type is most appropriate for this project?
n: Driven piles install quickly through loose alluvium and give high capacity and settlement control without soil improvement. Source: Das, Principles of Foundation Engineering, Ch. 9.

q: A low-rise commercial structure is planned on a site where the geotechnical report shows a uniform soi! profile with adequate bearing capacity, minimal differential settlement risk, and well-spaced columns carrying moderate axial loads. The structural engineer must select the most economical foundation type for each individual column. Which foundation system is most appropriate for these conditions?
n: Isolated (spread) footings are the most economical choice for well-spaced columns with moderate loads on good, uniform soil. Source: Das, Principles of Foundation Engineering, Ch. 3.

q: A proposed 5-storey mixed-use building will be constructed on a site underlain by a thick layer of soft, low-bearing-capacity clay with highly variable
n: A mat foundation spreads loads over a large area, which suits thick soft clay with variable N-values. Source: Das, Principles of Foundation Engineering, Ch. 6.

q: During a site layout review, the engineer discovers that two adjacent columns are so close to a property line that providing two separate isolated footings would cause one footing to extend beyond the lot boundary. To support both columns safely while keeping the foundation within the allowable footprint, which foundation system should be used?
n: A combined footing supports two closely spaced columns on one footing. It keeps the foundation inside the property line. Source: Das, Principles of Foundation Engineering, Ch. 6 (Combined Footings).

q: A two-storey commercial building is designed with long, continuous load-bearing CHB walls. The soil report shows a uniform layer of medium-dense sandy clay with no significant differential settlement risk. The engineer must select the most economical foundation type that can support continuous wall loads along their entire length. Which foundation system is most appropriate?
n: Continuous load-bearing walls on uniform, adequate soil are most economically supported on strip footings. Source: Das, Principles of Foundation Engineering, Ch. 3.

q: A site investigation reveals a shallow layer of very weak soil overlying firm strata at depth. The structural design requires a wall to be supported even though the soil directly beneath it cannot provide adequate bearing capacity. The engineer decides to span the load between two pile caps so that the wall load bypasses the weak soil entirely. Which structural element is appropriate for this condition?
n: A grade beam spans between pile caps and carries the wall load past the weak soil beneath. Source: Das, Principles of Foundation Engineering, Ch. 9; Ching, Building Construction Illustrated.

q: During a foundation layout review, the engineer notices that two isolated footings supporting adjacent columns are experiencing different settlement tendencies due to slight soil variability. To prevent the footings from moving independently and to improve overall foundation stability, which structural element should be used to connect the footings without carrying vertical wall or column loads?
n: A tie beam links isolated footings so they act together and do not move independently. It carries no vertical wall or column load. Source: NSCP 2015 (7th ed.), Vol. 1, Sec. 418.13.

q: Which type of foundation system is most effective for flood-prone areas, ensuring stability, erosion resistance and structural longevity?
n: In flood-prone, erodible ground, piles reach below the scour and erosion depth, giving stable, long-lasting support. Source: FEMA P-55, Coastal Construction Manual (pile foundations in flood zones).

q: Which type of footing is typically used to support vertical elements such as poles, towers, or columns with symmetrical cross-sections, offering uniform load distribution in all directions?
n: Circular footings suit symmetrical vertical elements such as poles, towers and round columns. They distribute load evenly in all directions. Source: Das, Principles of Foundation Engineering, Ch. 3.

q: Which type of foundation provides continuous structural support along the base of a load-bearing wall, ensuring uniform settlement control, optimized bearing pressure distribution and compliance with geotechnical stability requirements?
n: A strip footing gives continuous support along a load-bearing wall and spreads its pressure evenly. Source: Das, Principles of Foundation Engineering, Ch. 3.

q: A type of footing adopted when heavy structures are to be constructed on soft or marshy sites. It is also known as mat foundation.
n: A raft (mat) foundation is used for heavy structures on soft or marshy sites. Source: Das, Principles of Foundation Engineering, Ch. 6.

q: Recommended foundation when the spacing between the footing is greater than usual and there is a need to connect two or more footings due to eccentric loads. It is typically used at property boundaries where the column distance from the boundary is very small.
n: A strap footing ties an eccentrically loaded boundary footing to an interior footing with a strap beam. It is used when a column sits very close to the property line. Source: Das, Principles of Foundation Engineering, Ch. 6 (Strap/Cantilever Footings).

q: Recommended footing when ground bearing capacity is low and heavy columns are closely spaced
n: Low bearing capacity with heavy, closely spaced columns calls for a mat footing. Source: Das, Principles of Foundation Engineering, Ch. 6.

q: When the columns in a row are too close to each other such that their individual footing will overlap with each other, we will use
n: When columns in a row are so close that their footings would overlap, one continuous footing is used under the row. Source: Das, Principles of Foundation Engineering, Ch. 3 and 6.

q: What footing to design to support two parallel columns?
n: Two parallel, adjacent columns are supported on a combined footing. Source: Das, Principles of Foundation Engineering, Ch. 6 (Combined Footings).

q: A footing that supports two or more columns
n: A combined footing supports two or more columns. Source: Das, Principles of Foundation Engineering, Ch. 6.

q: Which of the following shapes is most commonly used for an isolated footing supporting a single column?
n: Isolated footings under single concentric columns are usually square, giving equal projection and pressure all around. Source: Das, Principles of Foundation Engineering, Ch. 3; Ching, Building Construction Illustrated.

q: Which type of settlement occurs in non-uniform, alluvial deposits or poorly compacted fill, and is the most common cause of structural damage?
n: Differential settlement happens when parts of a foundation settle by different amounts, typically on non-uniform alluvial deposits or poorly compacted fill. It distorts the frame and is the most common cause of structural damage. Source: Das, Principles of Foundation Engineering, Ch. 5 (Settlement); Ching, Building Construction Illustrated, Ch. 3.

q: Which type of settlement is the most critical in foundation design?
n: Differential settlement is the critical case in foundation design because the uneven movement induces distortion, cracking and added stresses in the superstructure. Uniform settlement is generally harmless. Source: Das, Principles of Foundation Engineering, Ch. 5; NSCP 2015, Ch. 3 (Foundations).

q: Which type of settlement is a special case of differential settlement that is often caused by eccentric loads or localized weak soil zones, and leads to door misalignment and window jamming?
n: Tipping (tilting or angular) settlement is a special case of differential settlement. The structure rotates as a unit, often from eccentric loads or a localized weak soil zone, so doors misalign and windows jam. Source: Das, Principles of Foundation Engineering, Ch. 5 (Angular Distortion).

q: Which type of settlement is characterized by the downward movement of the foundation by the same amount, with no distortion and no cracks, and is usually not structurally harmful? It is common in well-compacted and uniform soil layers.
n: In uniform settlement, the whole foundation moves down by the same amount. There is no distortion or cracking, so it is usually not structurally harmful. It is common on well-compacted, uniform soil. Source: Das, Principles of Foundation Engineering, Ch. 5.

q: A building exhibits settlement such that one side of the foundation experiences greater downward movement than the other, resulting in a noticeable lean. Despite the unequal settlement, the superstructure remains largely free from major cracks. Based on the settlement patterns illustrated, which classification most accurately describes the condition?
o: Differential Settlement, because unequal foundation movement automatically produces structural cracking.
Tilting Settlement, because the structure rotates as a unit due to non-uniform support conditions.
Uniform Settlement, because all portions of the structure remain structurally connected.
Differential Settlement with Distortion, because any foundation rotation necessarily causes deformation of the superstructure.
n: One side settling more so that the whole building leans as a unit, without much cracking, is tilting (rotational) settlement. Source: Das, Principles of Foundation Engineering, Ch. 5 (Settlement; tilt and angular distortion).

q: What is the primary purpose of reinforcing bars in a concrete footing when considering structural stability under load?
o: To counteract tensile stresses that develop due to bending moments and soil interaction
To enhance compressive strength, ensuring the footing resists downward forces more effectively
To evenly distribute vertical loads across the footing, reducing localized pressure points
To prevent lateral displacement of the footing, maintaining its fixed position in weak soils
n: Footings bend upward between the column and the soil pressure. The bars resist the tension at the bottom face. Source: NSCP 2015 (7th ed.), Vol. 1, Sec. 413.3 (footing design).

q: A proposed 7-storey nursing home is being evaluated for two facade options: a full glass curtain wall system or a traditional masonry exterior wall. The structural engineer explains that the choice will influence the required footing size because of differences in dead load and seismic mass, which are critical for a building housing elderly occupants. Which statement best describes this impact?
o: The footing will be larger with masonry because its higher dead load and seismic mass increase foundation demand
The footing will be smaller with masonry because its added stiffness reduces foundation loads
The footing will be larger with a curtain wall because its lighter weight increases lateral drift
The footing size will be the same because facade materials do not significantly affect gravity loads on the foundation
n: Masonry is much heavier than glass. The extra dead load and seismic mass raise both gravity and seismic demand on the footings, so they get bigger. Source: NSCP 2015 (7th ed.), Vol. 1, Secs. 204 (dead loads) and 208 (seismic weight W).

q: Under the IRR of the National Building Code of the Philippines (NBCP). Group A residential dwellings may follow prescriptive foundation dimensions instead of full structural design. For these structures, what is the minimum required thickness of concrete footings as specified in the Code's prescriptive provisions?
n: For Group A dwellings, footings must be at least 250 mm thick. Source: NBC (PD 1096) IRR, Rule VIII (Group A dwellings), Foundation (footings at least 250 mm thick and 600 mm below grade).

q: As per NBCP, footings for Group A dwellings should be at least how many millimeters below the surface of the ground?
n: Group A dwelling footings must be at least 600 mm below the ground surface. Source: NBC (PD 1096) IRR, Rule VIII (Group A dwellings), Foundation.

q: Which is often used on a sloping site where the foundation follows the slope without too much excavation?
n: Stepped footings follow a sloping site in level steps, avoiding heavy excavation. Source: Ching, Building Construction Illustrated; Das, Principles of Foundation Engineering, Ch. 3.

q: Before commencing excavation work, how many days in advance must the person responsible notify the owners of adjoining buildings in writing, according to NSCP requirements?
n: Whoever is responsible for an excavation must notify the owners of adjoining buildings in writing at least ten days beforehand. Source: NBC (PD 1096) IRR, Rule XI, Sec. 1108 (protection of adjoining property); NSCP 2015, Sec. 304 (excavation and fill).

q: Footing should not rest on
n: Footings must rest on undisturbed natural soil or properly engineered fill. Ordinary earth fill can settle unevenly. Source: NSCP 2015 (7th ed.), Vol. 1, Sec. 304 (Excavation and Fills); Das, Principles of Foundation Engineering, Ch. 3.

q: Which type of soil from the choices has the weakest bearing capacity?
n: Peat is highly organic, compressible and very weak. It has the lowest bearing capacity of these and is unsuitable for foundations. Source: Das, Principles of Foundation Engineering, Ch. 1 (Organic soils); NSCP 2015, Table 304-1.

q: From among the choices, which would be best for a 2-storey structure?
n: Among loam, silt, clay and sand, sand (especially dense, well-graded) has the highest bearing capacity and least settlement, so it best suits a 2-storey building. Source: NSCP 2015, Table 304-1 (allowable foundation pressures).

q: Which foundation would you use to distribute the heavy load of the building when the soil is weak?
n: A mat foundation spreads a heavy building's load over its whole footprint, lowering bearing pressure on weak soil. Source: Das, Principles of Foundation Engineering, Ch. 6.

q: Which is a type of shallow foundation used when we are certain that there would be no varying settlement as the bearing capacity of the soil is within the required design load.
n: Isolated (spread) footings are used when the soil safely carries the design loads and differential settlement is not expected. Source: Das, Principles of Foundation Engineering, Ch. 3.

q: Which geotechnical test is most suited for evaluating soil bearing capacity using a dynamic impact-driven mechanism, where a drop hammer drives a split-barrel sampler into boreholes to assess in-situ density and relative strength?
n: In the SPT, a 63.5 kg drop hammer drives a split-barrel sampler. The blow count (N) indicates in-situ density and relative strength. Source: ASTM D1586 (Standard Penetration Test).

q: During a geotechnical investigation for a proposed mid-rise structure on a sloping site, the design team needed an in-situ test that could provide both soil stratification and an index of soil resistance to penetration, expressed in terms of "N-values." Which field test is typically conducted to obtain this information?
n: The SPT recovers samples (showing stratification) and gives N-values as an index of penetration resistance. Source: ASTM D1586.

q: A geotechnical team is investigating a potential foundation failure along a mountainous access road. The design requires a field test capable of directly determining the soil's allowable bearing capacity by applying incremental loads and measuring the resulting settlements at the actual foundation level. Which test provides this direct evaluation?
n: A plate load test applies load in increments to a steel plate at foundation level and measures settlement. It directly evaluates bearing capacity. Source: ASTM D1194 / IS 1888 (Plate Load Test).

q: During a forensic geotechnical investigation of a failed retaining wall, the engineering team needed to determine the natural moisture content of the backfill to evaluate whether saturation contributed to the loss of shear strength. Which of the following tests is the standard laboratory method used-to. accurately measure the moisture content of soil?
n: The standard laboratory method for moisture content is oven-drying at 110 ± 5 °C to constant mass. Source: ASTM D2216.

q: What do you call the mechanical removal of earth material?
n: Excavation is the mechanical removal of earth material. Source: Ching, Building Construction Illustrated (site work).

q: Which site preparation process involves controlled earthmoving operations to establish precise elevation gradients, ensuring proper drainage flow paths, subgrade load distribution and compliance with construction tolerances?
n: Site grading shapes the ground to set elevations and slopes for drainage and to prepare the subgrade. Source: Ching, Building Construction Illustrated (site grading).
